title: 32-storey tower approved at 83-87 Weber Street East
subtitle: Affordable units and tower separation debated; in-camera decisions on an arts space operating agreement and a school board land exchange.
overview: Council approved an Official Plan amendment and zoning change for 83-87 Weber Street East, allowing a 32-storey mixed-use building with a floor space ratio of 18 {{vote:m1}}. Planning staff had recommended a shorter building, and the taller version was added through an amendment {{vote:m2}}. The Official Plan amendment goes to the Region of Waterloo for approval.

The applicant offered 26 affordable units for 20 years, larger unit sizes, a wider setback and an energy upgrade, and said construction could start next year. Staff said the taller design meets far less of the city's tall building separation guidelines. Several councillors said the process was not ideal and the public was left out of the late changes.

After a recess, council also acted on matters from its closed session. Council directed staff on an employee recruitment matter, authorized an interim operating agreement for 36 King Street West, and authorized a land exchange agreement with the Waterloo Catholic District School Board. The related by-laws were passed.

decisions.detail: Council adopted the Official Plan amendment and approved the zoning change for a 32-storey mixed-use building with a floor space ratio of 18, as amended.

decisions.item: Amendment for added height and density
decisions.detail: Council approved an amendment raising the building from 25 to 32 storeys and the floor space ratio from 14 to 18, with a clause that no further notice is required.
Council directed staff to proceed according to the in-camera direction in report COR-2023-484 on a labour relations matter.
Council authorized the Mayor and Clerk to sign an interim operating agreement with Green Light Arts for 36 King Street West, to the City Solicitor's satisfaction.
Council authorized an agreement of purchase and sale with the Waterloo Catholic District School Board for a land exchange, using the earlier terms plus revised terms discussed in closed session.

debate: Staff said the original recommendation struck a balance, and that the revised tower met only a fraction of the tall building separation guidelines. They said this could limit how neighbouring sites on the block are developed.
The applicant said it would hire a third-party engineer to assess an adjacent heritage property before and after construction. It also said nearby sites could still be developed as towers.

Supporters said the housing crisis, 26 affordable units for 20 years, larger units, energy upgrades and the developer's record of starting construction quickly outweighed the guideline shortfall. One councillor estimated the affordable units cost the developer over $2 million in lost rent.

Opponents said the process was a concern, with the public left out of late changes. One questioned who the affordable units would serve, given the province's coming changes to the definition of affordability.

Several councillors said they were struggling to balance staff's planning expertise and neighbours' wellbeing against urgent housing need. They also said future applications should be handled differently.
